say.text: Welcome to class two. Last time we asked what it means to define something. Today we try that on a word everybody uses: energy.

show.text: Energy: precise to calculate, slippery to explain

say.text: By the end, you can say what physicists mean by energy and name its main forms. You can also explain why 'energy is conserved' is a rule about bookkeeping, not about a substance.

show.text:
1. What physicists mean by energy
2. The main forms, and how energy moves between them
3. Why 'conserved' is bookkeeping
4. Where everyday talk goes wrong
5. Open questions

say.text: In daily life, energy is a feeling, a bill, or a fizzy drink. 'I have no energy today.' Physics took the word and gave it a narrower job.

show.text: energy (everyday): liveliness, power, get-up-and-go

say.text: To reach the physics meaning we need one more word: work. In physics, work means a force moving something over a distance.

show.text: Work = a force moves something over a distance

say.text: Lifting a book onto a shelf is work. Doing work on an object changes its energy, and the book now has more stored energy than before.

show.text: A hand lifting a book from a table up onto a high shelf.

ask.q: Which of these is work in the physics sense?
ask.right: Pushing a box across the floor
wrong: Holding a heavy bag still in the air
Thinking hard about a problem
Watching a ball sit on a table
ask.why: Physics work needs a force that moves something over a distance. Holding a bag still involves no movement, so it is not physics work, even though your muscles get tired.

say.text: So many textbooks say energy is the ability to do work. But OpenStax calls that a loose definition, because some energy can't be used to do work.

show.text: There is no simple, yet accurate, scientific definition for energy.

say.text: Other authors say the same. Halliday and colleagues call a simple definition very difficult. Çengel and Boles say we all have a feeling for it, but a precise definition is hard.

show.text:
Halliday et al.: very difficult to give a simple definition
Çengel and Boles: everyone has a feeling for it; a precise definition is hard
Bergmann and Schaefer: nobody knows what energy really is

say.text: Richard Feynman said it most sharply. He did not mean physicists can't use energy, because they use it all the time. He meant we have no picture of what it is made of, such as little blobs of fixed size.

show.text: It is important to realize that in physics today we have no knowledge of what energy is.

say.text: So what do physicists have instead of a one-line definition? They have a rule. A certain number, which we call energy, stays the same through all the changes nature makes, as long as nothing enters or leaves.

show.text: Energy: a number that stays the same (conserved)

say.text: Feynman made this clear with a story. A child has 28 blocks that can't be broken or destroyed. Each evening his mother counts them and finds 28.

show.text: Illustration: 28 indestructible blocks

say.text: One day there are only 26. Another day there are 30. The 30 turns out to be Bruce's blocks, left behind after a visit. The count only stays at 28 if you check that nothing came in or went out.

show.text:
Day 1: 28 blocks
A later day: 26 blocks
Another day: 30 blocks (some of Bruce's were left behind)
The rule: nothing in, nothing out, same total

say.text: Here is the key point. In Feynman's story about energy, there are no blocks. Energy has no tiny pieces to count. It is a number we work out, and the number stays put.

show.text: There are no blocks: energy is a calculated number

ask.q: In Feynman's story, what does the number 28 stand for?
ask.right: The total energy: a number we calculate, not a count of tiny pieces
wrong: How many tiny packets of energy are in the room
How many forms of energy there are
How many days the mother counted
ask.why: Feynman said the remarkable thing about the picture is that there are no blocks. Energy is an abstract quantity we calculate. It is not a pile of little things.

say.text: That is why we call it bookkeeping. Think of a sealed bank account: money moves between pockets, but the total doesn't change. And this rule isn't just a guess, because it is based on experiment.

show.text:
Substance picture (not how physics treats energy): a stuff that fills things up and flows like water.
Bookkeeping picture: a number we calculate for a system, which stays the same when nothing enters or leaves.

say.text: Now the forms. Feynman listed nine: gravitational, kinetic, heat, elastic, electrical, chemical, radiant, nuclear, and mass energy. Each form is a different way the same total shows up.

show.text:
Gravitational
Kinetic (motion)
Heat
Elastic
Electrical
Chemical
Radiant (light)
Nuclear
Mass

say.text: Most forms fall into two families. Potential energy is stored energy, like chemical energy held in the bonds of a battery or a fuel. Kinetic energy is the energy of movement, and heat is the jostling of atoms.

show.text:
Potential (stored): chemical energy in food, fuel and batteries; the energy of position.
Kinetic (movement): a moving car; heat, which comes from atoms and molecules moving.

say.text: Energy keeps changing form. Coal's chemical energy becomes heat as it burns, and the heat boils water. In a leaf, light becomes chemical energy. The form changes, but the total doesn't.

show.text:
Coal: chemical → thermal (heat) → steam
Leaf: light (radiant) → chemical
Food in your body: chemical → thermal, and movement

ask.q: A plant uses sunlight to make sugar. Which change of form is that?
wrong: Chemical energy into light
Kinetic energy into heat
Heat into electrical energy
ask.why: In photosynthesis, light energy is converted into chemical energy stored in the plant.

say.text: Why is energy conserved at all? In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether showed it is linked to a symmetry. Run an experiment today or next week and the laws of physics give the same results, because they don't change as time passes.

show.text:
The laws of physics don't change over time (time-translation symmetry)
↔ The total energy of a system is conserved

say.text: That also tells us the rule's limits. A system that breaks time symmetry can break energy conservation along with it. Keep that in mind, because we'll meet it at the end.

show.text: No time symmetry → no guaranteed energy conservation

ask.q: According to Noether's result, energy conservation is linked to which fact?
ask.right: The laws of physics not changing as time passes
wrong: Energy being a fluid that flows around
Machines being 100% efficient
Temperature staying the same
ask.why: Noether showed that time-translation symmetry, meaning the laws don't change over time, corresponds to conservation of total energy.

say.text: Now where everyday talk goes wrong. First: 'energy is running out.' The total amount of energy never changes. But in every change, some of it ends up as low-grade heat that we can't easily use again, so we say it was 'used up.'

show.text: Not 'used up': changed into forms we can't easily use

ask.q: A torch battery goes flat. Which is the best physics description?
ask.right: The energy was changed into other forms, mostly heat, that are hard to use again
wrong: The energy was destroyed
The energy left the universe
The battery made the energy into brand-new energy
ask.why: The total amount of energy never changes. In practice, much of it ends up as low-grade heat that can't easily do more work, which is why people say it was 'used up'.

say.text: Second: the word 'conserve' has two meanings. In physics, conserved means the total stays constant. In daily life, conserving energy means saving the usable kinds, so we use less fuel and electricity.

show.text:
Physics: the total is conserved, so it never changes.
Everyday: 'conserve' means using less of the usable forms.

say.text: Third: 'positive energy.' In physics, positive and negative are signs in a calculation. Atoms held together, for example, have negative energy, equal to what you'd have to put in to pull them apart.

show.text: Physics: positive or negative = the sign of a calculated number

ask.q: In physics, what does 'negative energy' mean for two things held together?
ask.right: You would have to put energy in to pull them apart
wrong: They are made of antimatter
They have lost their energy for good
They are in a bad mood
ask.why: For bound things, the negative energy equals the energy you must supply to separate them. It is a sign in a calculation. The wellness phrase 'positive energy' is a different use of the word, and it is not this quantity.

say.text: Now the open questions. In the late 1990s astronomers found that the universe's expansion is speeding up. Whatever causes this is called dark energy, and NASA estimates it is about 68 percent of the universe.
Here is the full picture. NASA's split is 5 percent ordinary matter, 27 percent dark matter and 68 percent dark energy. Scientists know even less about dark energy than about dark matter.

show.text: What the universe is made of (NASA estimate)

say.text: One idea is that dark energy is vacuum energy, a background energy of empty space. It could equal the cosmological constant, a term in Einstein's equations. New telescopes are now testing these ideas.

show.text: Dark energy: vacuum energy? Still unknown.

say.text: Now the puzzle that links back to Noether. Her rule needs time symmetry, but an expanding universe is different from one moment to the next. Many cosmologists conclude there is no single total energy for the whole universe that stays constant.

show.text:
Everyday lab: the laws and set-up don't change with time, so energy is conserved.
Expanding universe: space itself changes with time, so a total energy that stays constant isn't defined.

ask.q: Why do many cosmologists say there is no conserved total energy for the whole expanding universe?
ask.right: The rule depends on time symmetry, and an expanding universe changes from moment to moment
wrong: Dark energy is stealing the energy
Noether's theorem was proven wrong
Energy is a fluid that leaks out of space
ask.why: Energy conservation follows from time-translation symmetry. Expansion breaks that symmetry, so no total energy exists that is guaranteed to stay constant. The rule isn't broken, because its condition isn't met.

say.text: Careful: this does not mean energy vanishes in everyday life. Locally, at each point and in each interaction, energy is still conserved. When light is stretched by expansion, its energy doesn't go anywhere. It is measured by observers who are moving away.

show.text:
Locally: energy conserved at every point and in every interaction
Whole expanding universe: no unambiguous total to conserve
Stretched light: energy goes nowhere; it is measured from a receding point of view

say.text: Let's gather it up. Energy is easy to calculate and hard to explain in one sentence. It is a number that stays the same when nothing enters or leaves. It shows up in many forms, and it is conserved because the laws don't change with time.

show.text:
Energy = a conserved number, not a stuff
Many forms, one total
Conserved because of time symmetry (Noether)
Open: dark energy, and energy on cosmic scales

ask.q: Which sentence best sums up 'energy is conserved'?
ask.right: A calculated total stays the same in a closed system, even as it changes form
wrong: Energy is a fluid that can never be used up
Energy can be reused again and again forever
Energy is conserved everywhere, at every scale, with no open questions
ask.why: Conservation is bookkeeping: a number we calculate stays constant when nothing enters or leaves. Usable energy can still be lost to heat, and on cosmic scales the rule is an open question. Next class: information.

notes.topic: Dark energy and cosmic energy conservation

other_side.claim: Energy is a bookkeeping number, not a stuff.
other_side.other_view: Physicists and teachers often talk about energy as if it were a substance that flows or is stored, or as a height in a 'well'. One research paper argues that experts mix both pictures. It says an exclusive substance picture is untenable once negative energies appear. The bookkeeping view is the careful one, but the substance picture is a useful shorthand and is widely used.

other_side.claim: Total energy is not conserved in the expanding universe.
other_side.other_view: This is contested. One paper says the question is controversial, and that in some universe models (such as de Sitter) a global energy can be conserved. Another says the answer depends on what we mean by energy and by 'conserved', which is hard to settle in general relativity. Many cosmologists still treat it as settled, because expansion breaks time symmetry.

other_side.claim: Energy is the ability to do work.
other_side.other_view: OpenStax uses this as a loose definition and admits that not all energy is available to do work. The Victorian Department of Education argues that it ignores low-grade heat, which can't be used to do work. This is one reason many authors prefer 'a conserved quantity' as the core idea.
